Revision 1.1 of the Divine D. circuit board arrived on Aug 10, 2026.

In January 2025, Liberux, a startup based in Madrid, Spain, announced its upcoming NEXX Linux phone based on the RK3588S with specs to make nerds salivate: 4×2.4GHz Cortex-A76, 4x Cortex-A55, Mali-G610 MP4 GPU, 32GB LPDDR4X RAM, 256GB eMMC, 5G modem and 3 hardware kill switches. In June 2025, Liberux started the crowdfunding for the phone, and a couple days later announced a modular and open architecture that would allow the RAM board with an FPC connector to be upgraded up to 32GB, the eMMC board with a standard socket to be upgraded up to 512GB, and the cellular modem with a custom adapter board to be replaced/upgraded. The price varied between €790 and €1310, depending on the selected configuration. In addition, the NEXX would have two USB-C 3.1 ports to facilitate the phone being used a convergent desktop PC and an AW8737SCSR amplifier and a 3.5mm audio jack for better analog audio.

The NEXX was a revolutionary design, promising to be the first phone in history with two USB ports and the first one with the RAM and eMMC on separate boards, so it could be upgraded and connected like a normal PC. Liberux was attempting to offer the first truly convergent smartphone that had the right software and hardware to replace a desktop PC, yet it hardly generated any headlines in the tech press. It only got 120 pre-orders in a month, which generated a tenth of the $1.7 million in crowdfunding that it needed. When its crowdfunding campaign failed, Liberux reported that it was negotiating with investors for raise the funds to build a prototype. However, its last post on the company’s Mastadon account was in November 2025 about “moving forward with new self-funding.” After 11 months of silence, it is looking increasingly doubtful that the NEXX will ever come to market.

There is more hope for the Dawndrums Divine D. phone, which is being produced by a startup in Tunisia. The startup has continued to make slow progress according to its Mastodon posts. They are now on the second revision of their main board and have produced a breakout board for debugging it. They are developing their own distro known as DawnOS, which is based on Mobian and planning to support both the Phosh and Plasma Mobile interfaces. They are asking for donations, but appear to be largely self funded at this point. Like the NEXX, the Divine D. also promises to be an outstanding convergent phone, supporting up to 32GB RAM and offering a separate HDMI port for video out. It also offers a LoRa (long-range radio) chip, and a pogo pin interface to add accessories to the phone.
Jolla shows that there is still demand for Linux phones

While the failed crowdfunding of the Liberux NEXX and the limited sales of the Furi Labs FLX1 would suggest that there isn’t much hope for Linux phones, it is important to keep in mind that these phones were poorly advertised and produced by unknown startups that had no prior track record, so people were reluctant to order them. Bitter experience with the Librem 5 refunds, the failures of the PinePhone Pro, and all the cancelled Linux mobile devices over the years, such as the Ubuntu Edge in 2013, the Firefox OS phones in 2015, the Jolla Tablet in 2015 and the Necunos NC_1 in 2019, has taught Linux enthusiasts to be cautious about crowdfunding mobile devices.

However, there are reasons to believe that there is quite a bit of pent-up demand for mobile Linux, and it only requires the right kind of promotion and a company with a credible track record to unlock it. Ironically, the company demonstrating that people still want to use Linux phones is tiny Jolla, which has somehow managed to survive over the years.

The Finnish engineers who used to work on Nokia’s MeeGo founded their own company named Jolla Oy in 2011 to keep developing that code as Sailfish OS. They took the FOSS parts of MeeGo and added their proprietary Silica interface based on Qt QML, which imitates the Swipe UI that Nokia had developed for Meego on the N900/N9. They also developed their own proprietary AlienDalvik to run Android apps inside Linux. Jolla deserves credit for developing libhybris and helping to maintain much of the code developed by Nokia, including the oFono telephony library and the Maliit virtual keyboard. Remarkably, the small Finnish company managed to survive nearly going bankrupt in late 2015, when it cancelled its crowdfunded Jolla Tablet, which caused many of its customers who preordered to lose their money. It split off its hardware operations into a separate company named Jolla-Devices, which sells now Sony smartphones with Sailfish OS preinstalled to the European market, plus Volla Phones with Ubuntu Touch and Pixels with GrapheneOS.

After killing off the original company in 2024, because it was majority owned by Russian investors, who were politically toxic due to the war in Ukraine, Jolla reemerged under a new company named JollaBoys that bought the old company’s assets from Jolla Oy. The new Jolla company has returned to the business of selling hardware. Jolla announced its Jolla C2 Community Phone in May 2024, and started delivering them two months later, which helped reestablish the credibility of the company. When Jolla started taking preorders for its new Jolla Phone on December 5, 2025, it sold out its crowdfunding goal of 2000 phones within the first 48 hours and 5000 phones within the first week. People were pre-ordering the Jolla Phone without having seen any reviews of the phone and not even knowing what processor it would contain. The phone, which initially cost $499 and now costs was €679, was marketed as containing 12GB RAM, 256GB storage, a user-replaceable battery and a physical privacy switch. Jolla’s advertising for the phone clearly struck a chord with European consumers, which proclaimed it to be a “Do It Together (DIT) Linux phone, shaped by the people who use it.” The Finnish company emphasized the independence of the phone from the rest of the mobile phone industry, stating on the order page: “The Jolla Phone is not based on Big Tech technology. It is governed by European privacy thinking and a community-led model.”

Jolla has sold 15,000 units of its phone as of August 2026 just by taking pre-orders for production batches from its web site, and it probably could have sold far more units if it had paid for advertising, expanded beyond the European market, and kept the phone in stock, so customers didn’t have to wait months for the next production batch. Clearly, there is an untapped market of people who are dissatisfied with the reigning Android/iOS duopoly.
The mobile industry is shutting down the AOSP alternative

Today the use of Linux is growing on the desktop. Many people are installing Linux on their PCs, because they have become disgusted by how Microsoft has turned Windows into an advertising platform for surveillance capitalism and a vehicle for AI slop. Rather than buying new PCs, a growing number of people have decided to install Linux, because support for Windows 10 has ended and they can’t upgrade their old PCs to Windows 11 due to Microsoft’s arbitrary TPM restrictions.

Likewise, many people are equally disenchanted with Android and iOS on their phones. More people have grown distrustful of the surveillance capitalism which undergirds the Android market and the restrictions and rising prices of Apple’s “walled garden” on the iPhone, yet the options to escape the smartphone duopoly keep shrinking. In the past, people who wanted to gain some control over their digital lives could unlock the bootloader on their phone and install an AOSP derivative such as LineageOS, /e/OS, CalyxOS or GrapheneOS, however the mobile phone industry is increasingly shutting off this escape valve.

Every year there are fewer Android phone models on the market which allow the bootloader to be unlocked. The rise of Chinese brands, which now control roughly 60% of the global smartphone market, has driven many of the traditional phones brands out of the market which did allow their bootloaders to be unlocked. Many of the phone brands that were mod-friendly, such as LG, BQ, LeEco, WileyFox, Essential and Razer, are now gone from the market, and other mod-friendly brands like Sony and HTC now have so few sales that they are no longer relevant in the global smartphone market. Huawei stopped allowing its bootloaders to be unlocked in 2018. In the last couple years, Samsung, ASUS and Realme all followed Huawei’s bad example and no longer allow their bootloaders to be unlocked. Xiaomi, which rose to fame as a mod-friendly brand, has recently implemented so many restrictions to obtain its unlock codes, that it is unlikely that modders will bother porting custom ROMs to future Xiaomi models.

As noted in my article on LineageOS statistics, the brands which have good policies for bootloader unlocking has shrunk from 42.5% to about 7% of the global smartphone market over the last couple years. The brands which allow their bootloaders to be unlocked (without major restrictions like Xiaomi) only sold about 87 million phones in 2025, including Lenovo/Motorola (60M), Google (12M), OnePlus (11.6M), Nothing (2M), GigaSet (>1M), Sony (400k), Fairphone (145k), SHIFT (10k), Teracube, Volla and Brax. Together those brands only represent 7% of the 1245.5 million total smartphones sold in 2025.

However, that is an overestimate, since most phone models never get good custom ROMs made for them. A good portion of Motorola and Google phones are sold through carriers, and many carriers like Verizon don’t allow their phones to ever be unlocked, even if they are no longer under contract. MediaTek Dimensity and UNISOC Tiger processors have gained market share in recent years, and those chipmakers don’t publish the source code for their kernels like Qualcomm does for its Snapdragon processors. A few brands that use MediaTek SoC’s, such as Motorola, Xiaomi, Volla, Gigaset, TeraCube and Brax, do publish their kernel code, but that code for many other MediaTek phones will never get published, nor will custom ROMs be made for them. UNISOC processors are basically black boxes for the modding community. The bootloaders of all phones with Apple A-series, Huawei Kirin and recent Samsung Exynos processors are locked, so the modding community is restricted to just Qualcomm Snapdragon, Google Tensor and some MediaTek Dimensity processors. Motorola and Xiaomi have switched most of their budget model lines from Snapdragon to MediaTek Dimensity processors, so they are harder to mod.

Aside from the Motorola Moto G05, which was released in Jan 2025 and replaced 8 months later by the G06, there has not been a single budget phone released by a major phone maker in 2025 or 2026 that has gained official support by LineageOS. Gaining official LineageOS support is important, because many of the other custom ROMs are based on LineageOS and only port to its officially supported models. Just looking at phone models with official LineageOS support which allow their bootloaders to be unlocked, only about 20 million or 2% of smarphones sold each year are good for installing custom ROMs.

The situation is about to get much worse. Sadly, Oppo just announced that it will pull its OnePlus brand from the North American and European markets. OnePlus phones will still be sold in India and China (where the bootloader can be unlocked if the user presents an official Chinese ID card), but OnePlus is essentially gone for the modding community. Nothing, which was a rising star in the modding world, has been losing sales. The London-based company denies rumors that it will pull out of a third of the countries where it currently sells phones, but confirms that it plans to cut 100 jobs, which comprise 12% of its workforce. At any rate, none of the phones which Nothing has released in the last two years have gained official LineageOS support.
Samsung has been making it more and more difficult to mod its phones over the last decade, so the Korean company’s decision to lock the bootloader for all its phones getting its ONE UI 8 interface wasn’t a surprise, but Xiaomi’s decision to start restricting its bootloader unlock codes was a major blow for the modding community. The only major global brand left for modding is Motorola, but there are only unofficial ports available for recent Motorola models, meaning that some things don’t work correctly or security patches aren’t being provided. Motorola promises to launch phones with GrapheneOS in 2027, but they will be flagship models which probably cost over $1000 and be limited to a few select countries.

Aside from the Motorola Moto G15 (released in December 2024), people are unlikely to find a new phone where they can install an official LineageOS port for sale in Africa, most of Latin America (except Mexico) and most of Asia (except India, Japan, Taiwan, Singapore and Malaysia). The only option to run a custom ROM in most of the world is to buy a used Motorola or Xiaomi phone from a couple years ago, such as the Moto G (2024), Moto G32, Moto G34, Moto G84, POCO F5, POCO F5 Pro, POCO F6 Pro or Redmi Note 13 Pro. There are more recent phones like the Moto Edge 70, which have unofficial LineageOS ports, but it is a gamble if they will ever be officially supported by LineageOS.

As Google has pushed phone makers to support their phones for longer, many companies have decided to collect more personal data from their users for better targeted advertising and for training artificial intelligences. The smartphone industry is moving away from a business model based on planned obsolescence toward one based on surveillance capitalism, and the phone makers don’t want their users to opt out of the system, so they have removed the option to unlock the bootloader and made it harder to gain root access. That way they can recoup the cost of providing more years of support for their phones by monetizing their users’ data.

In addition, Google has made it harder to maintain custom ROMs, because it has moved more and more functionality from AOSP into its proprietary libraries and services (starting with Android 4.1 in 2012), and largely abandoned the development of many of the free/open source apps in AOSP in favor of its proprietary apps. Starting with AOSP 16 in 2025, Google stopped including the device trees and driver binaries for Pixel devices in AOSP, so ROM developers no longer had target devices, where they could easily test out and adapt the latest versions of AOSP on running hardware. Now custom ROM developers have to do painful trial and error to make the device trees for Pixel phones just like all the other phone brands. Google also squashed the kernel’s commit history, which makes it very difficult for ROMs like GrapheneOS to create their own custom kernels, because they can’t easily take new features, bug fixes and security patches from Google’s kernels.

Given how the smartphone industry is locking down their hardware and pushing business models that are inimical to users’ privacy, there is increased opportunity for Linux phones to be marketed to people who want to escape the Android/iOS duopoly and surveillance capitalism.
Three types of Linux phones are now possible

In the past, it was much harder to bring a Linux phone to market, but now there are three viable types of Linux phones that can be brought to market, and all of them have better prospects than in the past. The first type is the pure Linux phone which runs a Linux kernel, like the Librem 5, Liberty, PinePhone and PinePhone Pro. These phones previously didn’t have the processing power to offer the functionality that people expect in a smartphone. They often lacked components such image signal processors, audio digital signal processors, hardware video encoders, Vulkan graphics, neural processors and encryption engines, or they lacked the FOSS drivers to support those components. The RK3588S and the upcoming RK3668, however, will give pure Linux phones the processing power to be viable alternatives to Android and iOS phones for the first time.

The pure Linux phone is the riskiest type because it requires the most investment in engineering the hardware. Companies can’t just modify a reference phone design from Qualcomm or MediaTek or call up a phone ODM and ask them to modify one of their existing designs. They have to work with a design house or ODM that has some experience with radio frequencies to custom design a phone with 2 to 3 times more components than a standard smartphone. This means many iterations of the circuit board to get it right, and some kernel work to use all those different chips. It will take a long time to get to market, which can lead to customer complaints and reputational loss if using crowdfunding to finance the dev work.

The benefit of the pure Linux approach is that it allows for true hardware kill switches that cut the current to separate components, rather than the use of pins on an integrated mobile SoC or software to turn off the WiFi/Bluetooth, cellular modem and GPS/GNSS. The second benefit is the ability to select components that have free/open source drivers, which allows for greater software freedom and more transparency to address security and privacy concerns. The use of proprietary blobs in the drivers often prevents the kernel from being upgraded because the blobs are often only compatible with a specific kernel version number, which allows the chipmakers to dictate the lifespan of devices. Another benefit of not using a reference design from an SoC maker or an ODM is the phone maker has full control over the design and can publish the schematics and board views for the circuit boards, so the hardware is as free as the software.

In the past, Qualcomm didn’t produce powerful Internet of Things processors with Linux support, but now it is possible to build a good Linux phone based on an Internet of Things processor, like the QCM6490 or QCM8850 with an integrated cellular modem. These Dragonwing processors are not as up-to-date as the latest Snapdragon processors, but most of them receive 10 years or 15 years of software support, and many of them will eventually get partial support in mainline Linux, so they can live on with community support after they are no longer supported by Qualcomm.

The third kind of Linux phone is built on an integrated mobile SoC, which runs a standard Linux stack on top of an Android kernel using libhybris to translate glib calls to Android’s Bionic. This used to not be a good option because Android SoC’s were not supported long enough for the long development cycles and lower annual sales of Linux phones, but now it is possible for the high-end processors that are getting 8 years of software support from Qualcomm and MediaTek.

This approach is the most economical way to bring a Linux phone to market, since many phone ODMs already have reference models available and are willing to work with phone sellers to tweak those models to their specifications. It is not impossible to work with an ODM to add privacy switches to a design, as Furi Labs demonstrated with its FLX1, but it takes longer to get a custom design to market, so it is important to select an SoC that gets 7 or 8 years of software support, so the phone will enjoy a reasonable lifespan.

It is no longer necessary for Linux phone companies to expend huge amounts of capital in developing mobile Linux, because there are now three good mobile interfaces—Phosh, Plasma Mobile and Lomiri—which offer a reasonably complete complement of applications, so hardware companies don’t need to risk bankruptcy developing the software like before. Because Phosh and now Plasma Mobile are based on a well-supported desktop stack and convergent applications, they will require much less work to maintain and it is easier and less costly to keep providing software updates for the phone. Companies offering Linux phones will still need to hire developers to work on things like power management and camera support, but they don’t have to bet the farm like Purism did with the Librem 5 or provide no software support as PINE64 did with the PinePhone and PinePhone Pro.

This reduction in software development costs, however, probably won’t result in more economical Linux phones. The shorter software support for the QMC4490 and the mid-range and low range Snapdragon and Dimensity processors rules out the making of an economical Linux phone. It is possible to make an upper mid-range Linux phone based on a Snapdragon 7 or Dimensity 8000 series processor, but it won’t support video out via DisplayPort Alt Mode over USB-C, so it can’t be used as a convergent PC, which is a major selling point for Linux phones. Given that the QMC6490 does support DisplayPort Alt Mode, it is probably the best option for making an upper mid-range phone.

Companies like Jolla, Furi Labs, Volla and Brax may choose to continue making mid-range Linux phones, but they will likely suffer from the same problem as the FLX1 and C2, where the Android kernel is unsupported and no longer getting security updates, so it is better to move up to a more expensive SoC that gets 8 years of support. Ideally, these companies will stop using MediaTek processors, and select Snapdragon processors that get partially supported in mainline Linux, so people can run a distro like Nura on them after they are no longer supported.
The real barrier holding back Linux phones is the companies

Now that the available SoC’s and software are no longer holding back the making of compelling Linux phones, the real barrier to creating a viable Linux phone market are the companies to make and sell those phones. There aren’t many companies with the experience and passion to make Linux phones, which historically have lost money.

PINE64 recently announced that it is pausing production of most of its devices due to the high prices of RAM and eMMC. Essentially PINE64 is admitting that it can’t raise the price of many of its products, because they don’t have the needed software support, so many people won’t pay elevated prices for them. It appears unlikely at this point that PINE64 will change its business model to pay for software developers to work on the kernels for its hardware, nor is it repairing its relationship with the distributions and volunteer developers who have abandoned the company, so it is unlikely to ever produce the rumored PinePhone 2 using the RK3566. In theory another community-based Linux hardware company could arise, that charges a bit more so it has the necessary funds to pay developers to work on the kernel support for the hardware, but it appears highly unlikely that another community-based hardware company like PINE64 will appear.

In contrast, Purism is clearly planning to produce a second version of its phone. In its July 2026 newsletter, Purism stated that it “is in the early stages of planning the Librem 5 v2 and Liberty 5 v2.” It is preparing a “crowdfunding campaign in the coming months” to “gauge customer interest and traction, which will help fund the production of our second version.” The problem is that Purism’s public reputation has been stained by its refusal to refund the Librem 5 backers who cancelled their orders. Refunding the 600 customers who are still waiting for their Librem 5 refunds would do a lot to restore the company’s public reputation, and it would cost the company less than $400k. Without taking that step, it seems unlikely that Purism will be able to crowdfund the “over $2 million” that it projects will be needed to produce its next Linux phone. Maybe Purism can charge a lesser amount (such as $99) to pre-order the phone, and then use those numbers to raise capital privately to develop the phone.

At any rate, the time and cost of producing the Librem 5 v2 will be much less than the first version of the phone, because Phosh and its applications have already been developed and the mainline Linux driver support for the RK3588S is already in a good state due to the last four years of work by Collabora. Hopefully, Purism will either provide funding or developers to help Collabora get the ISP and hardware video encoding working.

The challenge for Purism is that it also needs to finance the development of its next generation of Librem 14 notebook, Librem 11 tablet and Librem Mini. The Librem 11 and Mini are rebadged ODM designs, so they don’t require as much work, but the Librem 14 is a custom design, which requires quite a bit more work and financing to create. In addition, Purism reported in its July newsletter that it has been pre-approved to get over $50 million in funding from the CHIPS Act to develop a Librem Core-V processor based on the RISC-V architecture, which will be a huge undertaking for the tiny company which doesn’t have any prior experience in chip design. Presumably, Purism will have to raise some matching funds to get the government funding for its chip project. In other words, many projects will be competing for Purism’s attention in the future, and the Librem 5 v2 could be neglected and postponed in favor of other products.

Presumably Dawndrums will launch a crowdfunding campaign once it has a working prototype of its RK3588S-based phone to show to the public, but the company based in Tunis has been very tight lipped about its future plans to bring the phone to market. There has been no news from Furi Labs about a new phone model to follow the FLX1s+. The implementation of Ubuntu Touch on the BraX3 phone has been stalled for months, and it appears that Brax Technologies is depending on the UBports community to finish the porting work. Volla Phone continues to offer Ubuntu Touch as an alternative operating system on its phones, but the German company’s primary focus is on developing its own Volla OS, which is an AOSP derivative oriented toward privacy.

Jolla is making the right moves to create a viable Linux phone market. The Finnish company says that it plans to move to mass production of its Jolla Phone, so the phone will be in stock, and to offer the phone to the North American market. However, many in the Linux community will be reluctant to embrace Jolla’s phones, because of the proprietary software in its Silica interface and its AppSupport (aka AlienDalvik) to run Android apps. People who believe in free and open source software won’t want to buy a phone from a company that has been violating the GPL 2.0 license by not published the kernel code for its Jolla C2 and Jolla Phone. In addition, these phones use UNISOC and MediaTek processors that don’t have any mainline Linux support, and they will probably have short lifespans, since their kernel are unlikely to ever be upgraded.

A critical factor in the success of Linux phones is publicizing the phones to attract the niche customers who care about Linux, software freedom, privacy or security. Liberux appears to have failed because it did such a poor job of publicizing its future NEXX phone and didn’t attract enough crowdfunding. Furi Labs similarly has done a very poor job of publicizing its phone, so that most Linux enthusiasts have never heard of the phone. Likewise, Dawndrums has done a very poor job of publicizing it development work on a future RK3588S phone. In contrast, Jolla has very effectively used social media to market its Jolla Phone to European customers.

There are several dozen companies that sell Linux PCs, which could potentially expand into the Linux phone market. Most of those companies, however, don’t have experience in the design of custom hardware. Most of them use standard notebook designs from one of the ODM’s that make specialty notebooks such as Clevo or Tongfang. Most of these companies also don’t have much experience doing kernel work, so they are probably better off just using a standard Android design provided by a phone ODM and installing Linux on top of Halium, so they can use a well-tested Android kernel and drivers.

There are also a number of companies that make Linux single board computers (SBC’s), who could potentially jump into the Linux phone market. They have more experience in working with Chinese and Taiwanese companies to design and produce custom hardware. They are better equipped to undertake the engineering challenges of entering the Linux phone market, but most of them do a poor job of engaging the community. Many companies which sell Linux SBC’s don’t have public forums for their customers and do a poor job of using social media and online advertising to promote their products.

Public opinion surveys show that people are increasingly aware that they are losing their privacy online. Ipsos polls found that 79% of global respondants and 84% of American respondants express worry about their online privacy. A Malwarebytes survey found that 89% of consumers are concerned regarding corporate and AI data misuse. 62% of Americans in a YouGov poll report worrying about how much personal data third parties have about them online. If Linux phones can be created that provide the same functionality and ease of use as Android or iOS phones, they could tap into that huge potential market of consumers who wish to preserve their privacy online. In order to appeal to mainstream users, Linux phones will need to support the usage of Android apps through Waydroid or a similar solution. In the same way that Murena and iodé sell AOSP phones which block third party trackers, Linux phones need to incorporate similar software.

The conditions may be ripe for Linux phones, but it is unclear whether the companies selling Linux phones will take advantage of those conditions to create a viable alternative to the current Android/iOS duopoly. For the sake of software freedom, online privacy and the greater longevity of mobile devices, a concerted push is needed to promote mobile Linux.

items.text:
Fable took my jorb

Its true. In a manner of speaking. If LLMs had not reached Fable / Mythos tier of marketed intelligence, I'd probably still have a job with the place I used to be at. For a short while.

It wasn't that Fable was better at my job. As the last engineer, Fable was cheaper than my compensation. Evidently, it gave enough confidence to the last vestiges of leadership that they could coast until M&A.

I've been through layoffs driven by budget cuts. I had to mechanically justify "I need this person because this product I'm oversee is critical to the business and still needs ownership" against a budget ceiling. Those I trusted to build out a greenfield product had their positions eliminated. The status quo was more important to maintain than resolving our operational issues with the next generation of our infrastructure.

That first meeting crushed my soul. I heard my ears ring more violently than ever. The color drained from the world. I could barely walk straight.

And, the next day, I went to a house party with two of my reports present knowing that both of them would lose their job next week with zero notice.

I know first hand what it is like to know and later execute on a layoff.

Finally, it was my time. I've had grief several times expecting it to come earlier. When it finally came, I took it well for a few hours.

Then my heart went to over 100 bpm as the fear and doubt for my future set in. And it didn't ease off for over a week.

Do you know how hard it is to sleep when all you can hear is your own heartbeat? Do you know how hard it is to function with four effective hours of sleep when you offer your body ten? It is rough.

Several in my social circles are having difficulty too. Six or Seven in a DevOps interest group have been laid off or have received a layoff notice in the last month. Work at one of FAANG of all places and oops, you're not important now! Here's 6 months of severance, we're so nice. "Ship happens" oh right, we can't ship your stuff because of some material restriction or let you pick up a box with some dignity, so we destroyed your stuff. GLHF.

Then there's that hiring manager who interviewed me at another company who then got laid off one week later because the CEO made a substantively late "AI is changing how we develop software" article. And another who lost their whole team, despite actively interviewing people in the USA, because a top-down decision was to offshore again after AI assistance raised the capability of work for the less passionate, less experienced, and less costly workforce.

"AI took my job" is far more fun to say than "AI contributed to my role being eliminated."

The frontier models are not good enough to replace an experienced engineer. They still are not, even though the marketing by the US frontier labs (and their 'I quit because I'm scared' employees) scream of what's to come.

These models lack the taste that makes for effective product decision making. It is cheaper than ever for a product manager to say "Someone complains about this on reddit, let's implement it", while the tasteful leader says 'No, that's not what our product is. Making that means we commit to it for a long time and our customers really want {something else we already do, but not perfectly} instead.'

These models lack the foresight to predict consequences weeks, months, years down the line on decisions and commitments — in operating costs, complexity, accessibility, and affordability to the very customers the product is for. All those secondary things really matter in making a product successful and worth buying. The slop services out there omit these secondary things all the time and you can taste it.

And yet, models are evidently able to give Shopify the confidence to yeet react-native out into the ocean and reach back to native iOS and android apps, entirely machine-coded while overseen by otherwise experienced and tasteful software developers.

And, I agree with Shopify. Models are getting good enough where they can be driven step by step, with a carefully crafted harness, to reproduce and port the behaviors they've A/B tested into oblivion as humans. They can push a rock up a hill. Then up the next hill, and so on — when the technique can be measured and check-pointed.

Agents are terribly good at copying things across domains. Just look at Theo's "for the memes" typescript in rust port. It ported the ts-go code to rust. According to Theo, Opus 5.5 reproduced bugs from the go version in the rust version exactly. On the other hand, Astra (the rival to Fable), failed at something so familiar, well known, and well documented.

We're heading towards the end of the year and I still do not see how these copy-machines with "super intelligence" inside are going to replace humans. What they have done is convince those with money to spend differently on their fellow humans.

Anyway, I got something else now. I get to see screens like this all day:

items.text:
1

Seeing comes before words. The child looks and recognizes before it can speak.

But there is also another sense in which seeing comes before words. It is seeing which establishes our place in the surrounding world; we explain that world with words, but words can never undo the fact that we are surrounded by it. The relation between what we see and what we know is never settled. Each evening we see the sun set. We know that the earth is turning away from it. Yet the knowledge, the explanation, never quite fits the sight. The Surrealist painter Magritte commented on this always-present gap between words and seeing in a painting called The Key of Dreams.

The way we see things is affected by what we know or what we believe. In the Middle Ages when men believed in the physical existence of Hell the sight of fire must have meant something different from what it means today. Nevertheless their idea of Hell owed a lot to the sight of fire consuming and the ashes remaining - as well as to their experience of the pain of burns.

When in love, the sight of the beloved has a completeness which no words and no embrace can match : a completeness which only the act of making love can temporarily accommodate.

Yet this seeing which comes before words, and can never be quite covered by them, is not a question of mechanically reacting to stimuli. (It can only be thought of in this way if one isolates the small part of the process which concerns the eye's retina.) We only see what we look at. To look is an act of choice. As a result of this act, what we see is brought within our reach - though not necessarily within arm's reach. To touch something is to situate oneself in relation to it. (Close your eyes, move round the room and notice how the faculty of touch is like a static, limited form of sight.) We never look at just one thing; we are always looking at the relation between things and ourselves. Our vision is continually active, continually moving, continually holding things in a circle around itself, constituting what is present to us as we are.

Soon after we can see, we are aware that we can also be seen. The eye of the other combines with our own eye to make it fully credible that we are part of the visible world.

If we accept that we can see that hill over there, we propose that from that hill we can be seen. The reciprocal nature of vision is more fundamental than that of spoken dialogue. And often dialogue is an attempt to verbalize this - an attempt to explain how, either metaphorically or literally, 'you see things', and an attempt to discover how 'he sees things'.

In the sense in which we use the word in this book, all images are man-made.

An image is a sight which has been recreated or reproduced. It is an appearance, or a set of appearances, which has been detached from the place and time in which it first made its appearance and preserved - for a few moments or a few centuries. Every image embodies a way of seeing. Even a photograph. For photographs are not, as is often assumed, a mechanical record. Every time we look at a photograph, we are aware, however slightly, of the photographer selecting that sight from an infinity of other possible sights. This is true even in the most casual family snapshot. The photographer's way of seeing is reflected in his choice of subject. The painter's way of seeing is reconstituted by the marks he makes on the canvas or paper. Yet, although every image embodies a way of seeing, our perception or appreciation of an image depends also upon our own way of seeing. (It may be, for example, that Sheila is one figure among twenty; but for our own reasons she is the one we have eyes for.)

Images were first made to conjure up the appearances of something that was absent. Gradually it became evident that an image could outlast what it represented; it then showed how something or somebody had once looked - and thus by implication how the subject had once been seen by other people. Later still the specific vision of the image-maker was also recognized as part of the record. An image became a record of how X had seen V. This was the result of an increasing consciousness of individuality, accompanying an increasing awareness of history. It would be rash to try to date this last development precisely. But certainly in Europe such consciousness has existed since the beginning of the Renaissance.

No other kind of relic or text from the past can offer such a direct testimony about the world which surrounded other people at other times. In this respect images are more precise and richer than literature. To say this is not to deny the expressive or imaginative quality of art, treating it as mere documentary evidence; the more imaginative the work, the more profoundly it allows us to share the artist's experience of the visible.

Yet when an image is presented as a work of art, the way people look at it is affected by a whole series of learnt assumptions about art. Assumptions concerning

Beauty

Truth

Genius

Civilization

Form

Status

Taste,

etc.

Many of these assumptions no longer accord with the world as it is. (The world-as-it-is is more than pure objective fact, it includes consciousness.) Out of true with the present, these assumptions obscure the past. They mystify rather than clarify. The past is never there waiting to be discovered, to be recognized for exactly what it is. History always constitutes the relation between a present and its past. Consequently fear of the present leads to mystification of the past. The past is not for living in; it is a well of conclusions from which we draw in order to act. Cultural mystification of the past entails a double loss. Works of art are made unnecessarily remote. And the past offers us fewer conclusions to complete in action.

When we 'see' a landscape, we situate ourselves in it. If we 'saw' the art of the past, we would situate ourselves in history. When we are prevented from seeing it, we are being deprived of the history which belongs to us. Who benefits from this deprivation? In the end, the art of the past is being mystified because a privileged minority is striving to invent a history which can retrospectively justify the role of the ruling classes, and such a justification can no longer make sense in modern terms. And so, inevitably, it mystifies.

Let us consider a typical example of such mystification. A two-volume study was recently published on Frans Hals.' It is the authoritative work to date on this painter. As a book of specialized art history it is no better and no worse than the average.

The last two great paintings by Frans Hals portray the Governors and the Governesses of an Alms House for old paupers in the Dutch seventeenth-century city of Haarlem. They were officially commissioned portraits. Hals, an old man of over eighty, was destitute. Most of his life he had been in debt. During the winter of 1664, the year he began painting these pictures, he obtained three loads of peat on public charity, otherwise he would have frozen to death. Those who now sat for him were administrators of such public charity.

The author records these facts and then explicitly says that it would be incorrect to read into the paintings any criticism of the sitters. There is no evidence, he says, that Hals painted them in a spirit of bitterness. The author considers them, however, remarkable works of art and explains why. Here he writes of the Regentesses:

Each woman speaks to us of the human condition with equal importance. Each woman stands out with equal clarity against the enormous dark surface, yet they are linked by a firm rhythmical arrangement and the subdued diagonal pattern formed by their heads and hands. Subtle modulations of the deep, glowing blacks contribute to the harmonious fusion of the whole and form an unforgettable contrast with the powerful whites and vivid flesh tones where the detached strokes reach a peak of breadth and strength. (our italics)

The compositional unity of a painting contributes fundamentally to the power of its image. It is reasonable to consider a painting's composition. But here the composition is written about as though it were in itself the emotional charge of the painting. Terms like harmonious fusion, unforgettable contrast, reaching a peak of breadth and strength transfer the emotion provoked by the image from the plane of lived experience, to that of disinterested 'art appreciation'. All conflict disappears. One is left with the unchanging 'human condition', and the painting considered as a marvellously made object.

Very little is known about Hals or the Regents who commissioned him. It is not possible to produce circumstantial evidence to establish what their relations were. But there is the evidence of the paintings themselves: the evidence of a group of men and a group of women as seen by another man, the painter. Study this evidence and judge for yourself.

The art historian fears such direct judgement:

As in so many other pictures by Hals, the penetrating characterizations almost seduce us into believing that we know the personality traits and even the habits of the men and women portrayed.

What is this 'seduction' he writes of ? It is nothing less than the paintings working upon'us. They work upon us because we accept the way Hals saw his sitters. We do not accept this innocently. We accept it in so far as it corresponds to our own observation of people, gestures. faces, institutions. This is possible because we still live in a society of comparable social relations and moral values. And it is precisely this which gives the paintings their psychological and social urgency. It is this - not the painter's skill as a 'seducer' - which convinces us that we can know the people portrayed.

The author continues:
In the case of some critics the seduction has been a total success. It has, for example, been asserted that the Regent in the tipped slouch hat, which hardly covers any of his long, lank hair, and whose curiously set eyes do not focus, was shown in a drunken state.

This, he suggests, is a libel. He argues that it was a fashion at that time to wear hats on the side of the head. He cites medical opinion to prove that the Regent's expression could well be the result of a facial paralysis. He insists that the painting would have been unacceptable to the Regents if one of them had been portrayed drunk. One might go on discussing each of these points for pages. (Men in seventeenth-century Holland wore their hats on the side of their heads in order to be thought of as adventurous and pleasure-loving. Heavy drinking was an approved practice. Etcetera.) But such a discussion would take us even farther away from the only confrontation which matters and which the author is determined to evade.

In this confrontation the Regents and Regentesses stare at Hals, a destitute old painter who has lost his reputation and lives off public charity; he examines them through the eyes of a pauper who must nevertheless try to be objective, i.e., must try to surmount the way he sees as a pauper. This is the drama of these paintings. A drama of an ' unforgettable contrast '.

Mystification has little to do with the vocabulary used. Mystification is the process of explaining away what might otherwise be evident. Hals was the first portraitist to paint the new characters and expressions created by capitalism. He did in pictorial terms what Balzac did two centuries later in literature. Yet the author of the authoritative work on these paintings sums up the artist's achievement by referring to

Hals's unwavering commitment to his personal vision, which enriches our consciousness of our fellow men and heightens our awe for the ever-increasing power of the mighty impulses that enabled him to give us a close view of life's vital forces.

That is mystification.

In order to avoid mystifying the past (which can equally well suffer pseudo-Marxist mystification) let us now examine the particular relation which now exists, so far as pictorial images are concerned, between the present and the past. If we can see the present clearly enough, we shall ask the right questions of the past.

Today we see the art of the past as nobody saw it before. We actually perceive it in a different way.

This difference can be illustrated in terms of what was thought of as perspective. The convention of perspective, which is unique to European art and which was first established in the early Renaissance, centres everything on the eye of the beholder. It is like a beam from a lighthouse - only instead of light travelling outwards, appearances travel in. The conventions called those appearances reality. Perspective makes the single eye the centre of the visible world. Everything converges on to the eye as to the vanishing point of infinity. The visible world is arranged for the spectator as the universe was once thought to be arranged for God.

According to the convention of perspective there is no visual reciprocity. There is no need for God to situate himself in relation to others: he is himself the situation. The inherent contradiction in perspective was that it structured all images of reality to address a single spectator who, unlike God, could only be in one place at a time.

After the invention of the camera this contradiction gradually became apparent.

This quotation is from an article written in 1923 by Dziga Veritov, the revolutionary Soviet film director

I'm an eye. A mechanical eye. I, the machine, show you a world the way only I can see it. I free myself for today and forever from human immobility. I'm in constant movement. I approach and pull away from objects. I creep under them. i move alongside a running horse's mouth. I fall and rise with the falling and rising bodies. This is I, the machine, manoeuvring in the chaotic movements, recording one movement after another in the most complex combinations.
Freed from the boundaries of time and space, I co-ordinate any and all points of the universe, wherever I want them to be. My way leads towards the creation of a fresh perception of the world. Thus I explain in a new way the world unknown to you.*

The camera isolated momentary appearances and in so doing destroyed the idea that images were timeless. Or, to put it another way, the camera showed that the notion of time passing was inseparable from the experience of the visual (except in paintings). What you saw depended upon where you were when. What you saw was relative to your position in time and space. It was no longer possible to imagine everything converging on the human eye as on the vanishing point of infinity.

This is not to say that before the invention of the camera men believed that everyone could see everything. But perspective organized the visual field as though that were indeed the ideal. Every drawing or painting that used perspective proposed to the spectator that he was the unique centre of the world. The camera - and more particularly the movie camera - demonstrated that there was no centre.

The invention of the camera changed the way men saw. The visible came to mean something different to them. This was immediately reflected in painting.

For the Impressionists the visible no longer presented itself to man in order to be seen. On the contrary, the visible, in continual flux, became fugitive. For the Cubists the visible was no longer what confronted the single eye, but the totality of possible views taken from points all round the object (or person) being depicted.

The invention of the camera also changed the way in which men saw paintings painted long before the camera was invented. Originally paintings were an integral part of the building for which they were designed. Sometimes in an early Renaissance church or chapel one has the feeling that the images on the wall are records of the building's interior life, that together they make up the building's memory - so much are they part of the particularity of the building.

The uniqueness of every painting was once part of the uniqueness of the place where it resided. Sometimes the painting was transportable. But it could never be seen in two places at the same time. When the camera reproduces a painting, it destroys the uniqueness of its image. As a result its meaning changes. Or, more exactly, its meaning multiplies and fragments into many meanings.

This is vividly illustrated by what happens when a painting is shown on a television screen. The painting enters each viewer's house. There it is surrounded by his wallpaper, his furniture, his mementoes. It enters the atmosphere of his family. It becomes their talking point. It lends its meaning to their meaning. At the same time it enters a million other houses and, in each of them, is seen in a different context. Because of the camera, the painting now travels to the spectator rather than the spectator to the painting. In its travels, its meaning is diversified.

One might argue that all reproductions more or less distort, and that therefore the original painting is still in a sense unique. Here is a reproduction of the Virgin of the Rocks by Leonardo da Vinci.

Having seen this reproduction, one can go to the National Gallery to look at the original and there discover what the reproduction lacks. Alternatively one can forget about the quality of the reproduction and simply be reminded, when one sees the original, that it is a famous painting of which somewhere one has already seen a reproduction. But in either case the uniqueness of the original now lies in it being the original of a reproduction. It is no longer what its image shows that strikes one as unique; its first meaning is no longer to be found in what it says, but in what it is.

This new status of the original work is the perfectly rational consequence of the new means of reproduction. But it is at this point that a process of mystification again enters. The meaning of the original work no longer lies in what it uniquely says but in what it uniquely is. How is its unique existence evaluated and defined in our present culture? It is defined as an object whose value depends upon its rarity. This value is affirmed and gauged by the price it fetches on the market. But because it is nevertheless 'a work of art' - and art is thought to be greater than commerce - its market price is said to be a reflection of its spiritual value. Yet the spiritual value of an object, as distinct from a message or an example, can only be explained in terms of magic or religion. And since in modern society neither of these is a living force, the art object, the 'work of art', is enveloped in an atmosphere of entirely bogus religiosity. Works of art are discussed and presented as though they were holy relics: relics which are first and foremost evidence of their own survival. The past in which they originated is studied in order to prove their survival genuine. They are declared art when their line of descent can be certified.

Before the Virgin of the Rocks the visitor to the National Gallery would be encouraged by nearly everything he might have heard and read about the painting to feel something like this: 'I am in front of it. I can see it. This painting by Leonardo is unlike any other in the world. The National Gallery has the real one. If I look at this painting hard enough, I should somehow be able to feel its authenticity. The Virgin of the Rocks by Leonardo da Vinci: it is authentic and therefore it is beautiful.'

To dismiss such feelings as naive would be quite wrong. They accord perfectly with the sophisticated culture of art experts for whom the National Gallery catalogue is written. The entry on the Virgin of the Rocks is one of the longest entries. It consists of fourteen closely printed pages. They do not deal with the meaning of the image. They deal with who commissioned the painting, legal squabbles, who owned it, its likely date, the families of its owners. Behind this information lie years of research. The aim of the research is to prove beyond any shadow of doubt that the painting is a genuine Leonardo. The secondary aim is to prove that an almost identical painting in the Louvre is a replica of the National Gallery version.

French art historians try to prove the opposite.

The National Gallery sells more reproductions of Leonardo's cartoon of The Virgin and Child with St Anne and St John the Baptist than any other picture in their collection. A few years ago it was known only to scholars. It became famous because an American wanted to buy it for two and a half million pounds.

Now it hangs in a room by itself. The room is like a chapel. The drawing is behind bullet-proof perspex. It has acquired a new kind of impressiveness. Not because of what it shows - not because of the meaning of its image. It has become impressive, mysterious, because of its market value.

The bogus religiosity which now surrounds original works of art, and which is ultimately dependent upon their market value, has become the substitute for what paintings lost when the camera made them reproducible. Its function is nostalgic. It is the final empty claim for the continuing values of an oligarchic, undemocratic culture. If the image is no longer unique and exclusive, the art object, the thing, must be made mysteriously so.

The majority of the population do not visit art museums. The following table shows how closely an interest in art is related to privileged education.

The majority take it as axiomatic that the museums are full of holy relics which refer to a mystery which excludes them: the mystery of unaccountable wealth. Or, to put this another way, they believe that original masterpieces belong to the preserve (both materially and spiritually) of the rich. Another table indicates what the idea of an art gallery suggests to each social class.

In the age of pictorial reproduction the meaning of paintings is no longer attached to them; their meaning becomes transmittable: that is to say it becomes information of a sort, and, like all information, it is either put to use or ignored; information carries no special authority within itself. When a painting is put to use, its meaning is either modified or totally changed. One should be quite clear about what this involves. It is not a question of reproduction failing to reproduce certain aspects of an image faithfully; it is a question of reproduction making it possible, even inevitable, that an image will be used for many different purposes and that the reproduced image, unlike an original work, can lend itself to them all. Let us examine some of the ways in which the reproduced image lends itself to such usage.

Reproduction isolates a detail of a painting from the whole. The detail is transformed. An allegorical figure becomes a portrait of a girl.

When a painting is reproduced by a film camera it inevitably becomes material for the film-maker's argument.

A film which reproduces images of a painting leads the spectator, through the painting, to the film-maker's own conclusions. The painting lends authority to the film-maker.

This is because a film unfolds in time and a painting does not.

In a film the way one image follows another, their succession, constructs an argument which becomes irreversible.

In a painting all its elements are there to be seen simultaneously. The spectator may need time to examine each element of the painting but whenever he reaches a conclusion, the simultaneity of the whole painting is there to reverse or qualify his conclusion. The painting maintains its own authority.

Paintings are often reproduced with words around them.

This is a landscape of a cornfield with birds flying out of it. Look at it for a moment. Then turn the page.

It is hard to define exactly how the words have changed the image but undoubtedly they have. The image now illustrates the sentence.

In this essay each image reproduced has become part of an argument which has little or nothing to do with the painting's original independent meaning. The words have quoted the paintings to confirm their own verbal authority. (The essays without words in this book may make that distinction clearer.)

Reproduced paintings, like all information, have to hold their own against all the other information being continually transmitted.

Consequently a reproduction, as well as making its own references to the image of its original, becomes itself the reference point for other images. The meaning of an image is changed according to what one sees immediately beside it or what comes immediately after it. Such authority as it retains, is distributed over the whole context in which it appears.

Because works of art are reproducible, they can, theoretically, be used by anybody. Yet mostly - in art books, magazines, films or within gilt frames in living-rooms - reproductions are still used to bolster the illusion that nothing has changed, that art, with its unique undiminished authority, justifies most other forms of authority, that art makes inequality seem noble and hierarchies seem thrilling. For example, the whole concept of the National Cultural Heritage exploits the authority of art to glorify the present social system and its priorities.

The means of reproduction are used politically and commercially to disguise or deny what their existence makes possible. But sometimes individuals use them differently.

Adults and children sometimes have boards in their bedrooms or living-rooms on which they pin pieces of paper: letters, snapshots, reproductions of paintings, newspaper cuttings, original drawings, postcards. On each board all the images belong to the same language and all are more or less equal within it, because they have been chosen in a highly personal way to match and express the experience of the room's inhabitant. Logically, these boards should replace museums.

What are we saying by that? Let us first be sure about what we are not saying.

We are not saying that there is nothing left to experience before original works of art except a sense of awe because they have survived. The way original works of art are usually approached - through museum catalogues, guides, hired cassettes, etc. - is not the only way they might be approached. When the art of the past ceases to be viewed nostalgically, the works will cease to be holy relics - although they will never re-become what they were before the age of reproduction. We are not saying original works of art are now useless.

Original paintings are silent and still in a sense that information never is. Even a reproduction hung on a wall is not comparable in this respect for in the original the silence and stillness permeate the actual material, the paint, in which one follows the traces of the painter's immediate gestures. This has the effect of closing the distance in time between the painting of the picture and one's own act of looking at it. In this special sense all paintings are contemporary. Hence the immediacy of their testimony. Their historical moment is literally there before our eyes. Cézanne made a similar observation from the painter's point of view. 'A minute in the world's life passes! To paint it in its reality, and forget everything for that! To become that minute, to be the sensitive plate . . . give the image of what we see, forgetting everything that has appeared before our time . . .' What we make of that painted moment when it is before our eyes depends upon what we expect of art, and that in turn depends today upon how we have already experienced the meaning of paintings through reproductions.

Or are we saying that all art can be understood spontaneously. We are not claiming that to cut out a magazine reproduction of an archaic Greek head, because it is reminiscent of some personal experience, and to pin it on to a board beside other disparate images, is to come to terms with the full meaning of that head.

The idea of innocence faces two ways. By refusing to enter a conspiracy, one remains innocent of that conspiracy. But to remain innocent may also be to remain ignorant. The issue is not between innocence and knowledge (or between the natural and the cultural) but between a total approach to art which attempts to relate it to every aspect of experience and the esoteric approach of a few specialized experts who are the clerks of the nostalgia of a ruling class in decline. (In decline, not before the proletariat, but before the new power of the corporation and the state.) The real question is: to whom does the meaning of the art of the past properly belong? To those who can apply it to their own lives, or to a cultural hierarchy of relic specialists?

The visual arts have always existed within a certain preserve; originally this preserve was magical or sacred. But it was also physical: it was the place, the cave, the building, in which, or for which, the work was made. The experience of art, which at first was the experience of ritual, was set apart from the rest of life - precisely in order to be able to exercise power over it. Later the preserve of art became a social one. It entered the culture of the ruling class, whilst physically it was set apart and isolated in their palaces and houses. During all this history the authority of art was inseparable from the particular authority of the preserve.

What the modem means of reproduction have done is to destroy the authority of art and to remove it - or, rather, to remove its images which they reproduce - from any preserve. For the first time ever, images of art have become ephemeral, ubiquitous, insubstantial, available, valueless, free. They surround us in the same way as a language surrounds us. They have entered the mainstream of life over which they no longer, in themselves, have power.

Yet very few people are aware of what has happened because the means of reproduction are used nearly all the time to promote
